title: HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication
summary: This informational RFC describes HMAC, a way to check that a message is authentic and unaltered by combining a secret shared key with a cryptographic hash function such as MD5 or SHA-1. Its strength depends on the underlying hash. HMAC is widely used in other protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: You and a friend share a secret stamp. Only someone with the stamp can mark a letter so it passes your check.

questions: what are ipad and opad in hmac
how long should an hmac key be
subtitle: A way to turn any ordinary hash function into a keyed integrity check that only holders of a shared secret can produce.

tldr.problem: Two parties that share a secret key need a way to check that data was not altered in transit, ideally using hash functions that already exist and run fast in software.
tldr.mechanism: HMAC hashes the message together with the key in two nested passes, using two fixed padding strings (ipad and opad) XORed into the key, and treats the hash function as an unmodified building block.
tldr.outcome: The strength of HMAC rests on the underlying hash function, which can be swapped for a better one later. The RFC is Informational and is updated by RFC 6151.

facts.label: Minimum truncated length
facts.value: Half the hash output and at least 80 bits

today: RFC 2104 is an Informational RFC and is updated by RFC 6151. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Keyed Hash
sections.content:
A message authentication code (MAC) lets two parties who share a secret key check that information sent between them, or stored, has not been changed. HMAC builds such a MAC out of a cryptographic hash function such as MD5 or SHA-1 plus a secret key.

The RFC lists the design goals: use available hash functions without modification, keep the hash function's original performance, handle keys in a simple way, have a well understood security analysis, and make it easy to replace the hash function if a faster or more secure one is needed.

The RFC writes the hash function as H. Specific versions are named after it, such as HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-MD5.
sections.plainLanguage: People wanted a way to prove a message was not tampered with, using a secret both sides know and tools that already exist, so nobody has to invent a brand new lock.

sections.title: The HMAC Computation
sections.content:
HMAC needs a hash function H that works by iterating a compression function over blocks of data, and a secret key K. The block length is B bytes (64 for MD5, SHA-1 and the other examples given) and the hash output length is L bytes (16 for MD5, 20 for SHA-1).

Two fixed strings are defined: ipad is the byte 0x36 repeated B times, and opad is the byte 0x5C repeated B times. The 'i' and 'o' stand for inner and outer. The result is H(K XOR opad, H(K XOR ipad, text)).

  • Pad the key with zero bytes to B bytes.
  • XOR that with ipad, append the message, and hash it.
  • XOR the padded key with opad, append the first hash result, and hash again to get the output.
sections.plainLanguage: Mix the secret with one special pattern and stamp the message once. Then mix the secret with a different pattern and stamp the first result again. The second stamp is your answer.

sections.title: Keys and Truncated Output
sections.content:
A key can be any length. Keys longer than B bytes are first hashed with H, and the resulting L-byte string is used as the key. Keys shorter than L bytes are strongly discouraged because they weaken the function. Longer keys are acceptable but do not add much strength, though they may help if the key's randomness is weak.

Keys need to be chosen at random (or from a cryptographically strong pseudo-random generator seeded with a random seed) and refreshed periodically. The RFC says current attacks do not indicate a specific frequency, but refreshing limits the damage of an exposed key.

An application may truncate the output to the leftmost t bits. The RFC recommends that t be not less than half the hash output length and not less than 80 bits. The truncated form is written HMAC-H-t, for example HMAC-SHA1-80.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick a long, random secret and change it now and then. You can also keep only the first part of the stamp, as long as you keep enough of it that nobody can guess it.

sections.title: Implementation Note
sections.content:
Because HMAC uses the hash function with its normal initial value (IV), the code of H needs no changes. If an implementer is willing to modify the hash code to accept a variable IV, there is an optional speed-up.

The intermediate results of the compression function on the blocks K XOR ipad and K XOR opad can be computed once, when the key is generated or before its first use, and then reused for each message. This saves two compression function calls per message, which matters most for short messages. The stored values must be protected like secret keys.

The RFC states that this is a local implementation choice and has no effect on interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: If you always use the same secret, you can do the first bit of work ahead of time and save it, as long as you keep that saved work just as secret.

sections.title: Security of HMAC
sections.content:
The security of HMAC depends on properties of the hash function: resistance to collision finding (in the case where the initial value is secret and random and the output is not available to the attacker), and the message authentication property of the compression function on single blocks. Because the construction does not depend on the details of H, it can be replaced by any other secure iterative hash function.

The RFC also points out that message authentication has a transient effect. If a scheme is broken, it gets replaced, but information authenticated in the past is not exposed, unlike encrypted data.

The strongest known attack is a birthday attack on collisions. For MD5 (16 bytes, 128 bits of output) the attacker would need correct tags on about 2**64 known plaintexts under the same key, which the RFC calls impossible in any realistic scenario. It stresses that this differs from ordinary collision attacks on a hash with no key.

The introduction notes that MD5 had recently been shown vulnerable to collision search attacks, which did not compromise its use inside HMAC as specified. SHA-1 appeared stronger, and users are told to watch for cryptanalytic developments and be ready to replace the hash.
sections.plainLanguage: Breaking the stamp would take an impossibly huge amount of tries. And if someone ever does break it, you just switch to a better stamp, and old letters stay as safe as they were.

data.title: HMAC definition
data.code:
ipad = the byte 0x36 repeated B times
opad = the byte 0x5C repeated B times

H(K XOR opad, H(K XOR ipad, text))
